name: The Joule Point: an Energy-Optimal Operating Point for AI Inference
problem: Data centres run GPU inference at full power by default, which maximises throughput but wastes energy per inference - and the inefficiency is a scheduling choice rather than a hardware limit.
mechanism: Characterises the GPU power-performance curve empirically: for a given workload, board power rises SUPERLINEARLY with the operating point, on top of a fixed power floor paid for as long as the job runs. Energy per inference is therefore U-shaped in the operating point (GPU, power cap), with a minimum the authors name the Joule Point at a cap of 43-46% of rated power. Because the optimum is nearly a per-card-type constant under load, a single static cap per card type captures nearly all of the saving, collapsing the online per-job search prior systems perform into a one-time characterisation.
speedup_reported: Capping to the Joule Point cuts energy per inference by roughly a quarter to a third versus uncapped operation, at a cost of each request running about 1.2x slower and holding aggregate throughput requiring that same ~1.2x factor more cards. Grounded in ELF, a dense power-cap dataset sweeping 20 inference models across 4 GPUs; replaying ELF in a fleet simulation under a power budget and capping each job to the least power meeting its deadline spends 18-45% less energy per served job. A single static cap per card type carries a mean penalty under one per cent versus the per-job optimum.
notes: REGARDLESS OF VENDOR AFFILIATION, THIS PAPER IS THE QUANTITATIVE COUNTERWEIGHT TO THE STANDARD 'RUN IT HOTTER, IT IS FASTER' ASSUMPTION IN AI-INFERENCE COST MODELS, and it is the single most decision-relevant measurement result in the power slice. Distinctive angle: it is a power-DELIVERY/power-cap physics characterisation (superlinear power-performance curve, fixed power floor), not an algorithmic efficiency result, and not a carbon-accounting or carbon-intensity study - so it sits in the datacentre-systems power-delivery line rather than the green-computing/energy-carbon literature. Caveats a reader must carry: the 43-46% figure is measured on 4 GPU types across 20 models and the authors themselves frame it as needing per-card-type characterisation; 'energy per inference' is measured, but the fleet-simulated 18-45% is a simulation replay rather than a deployed fleet. The 1.2x-latency-for-1.2x-cards tradeoff is the part that changes capital planning, because it says energy efficiency at this operating point is bought with hardware, not with software. Read alongside gotchas/idle-and-underbatched-fleet-can-cost-more-than-busy-fleet and gotchas/power-cap-cliff-at-300w-for-decode.
